summary.title: Repo-To-Skill: Distilling GitHub Repositories Into AI4AI Skills

details: Autonomous ML-research agents are described as backbone + harness, leaving domain 'operational knowledge' (which method/tool to use, when, and how to make it work) outside the agent, so it is rediscovered by trial and error in every task.
Relevant know-how exists only in declarative, human-oriented form (repositories, papers) that is too large to load into an agent's context.

DisCo: a skill-powered research agent operating in two modes over an unchanged backbone/harness — creator mode distills declarative sources into verified agent Skills, researcher mode loads them as operating context.

Skill distillation pipeline: anchor -> scope (capabilities) -> ground (evidence) -> construct candidate skill graph (SKILL.md interface + references/ + scripts/) -> verify/repair, with the anchor being either a source (task-agnostic) or a task (task-oriented); nothing is admitted without execution-backed verification.

Scaling this yields the AREX-Skill Library: 5,353 skills distilled from 1,000 widely used ML repositories, organized into 20 areas and 178 capability families behind a router enabling progressive disclosure.
1,000 ML repositories selected by open-source visibility/stars; one verified skill graph per repo built with GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6-sol at xhigh reasoning, ~$40 per repository.

Evidence boundary = repo source, docs, examples, tests, scripts, configs; verification via assertion-backed usability cases plus safe native tests/CLI/smoke checks, with localized repair and static gates (provenance, self-containment, no local-path leakage).

Two-level taxonomy induced by LLM pipeline from repo summaries only (stars/URLs/prior labels excluded), validated over 100 batches of 10 repos with separate locator and judge calls; final assignments made after freezing the tree; 2,209 exact repo-to-family assignments, 700 repos in multiple families.

PaperBench: 636 module-level skills from 153 prior papers (up to 10 related-work papers per target); target paper and its released code excluded; verification = isolated module tests plus bounded recovery experiment without the original repo.

MLE-bench: one descriptive (non-executable) skill graph per competition, built via task decomposition, web search (original competition page blocked), and diagnostic trials under a separate <=24 GPU-hour exploration budget.
FrontierCS: one frozen recovery-oriented graph shared across all tasks (entry router + 8 modules, 9 nodes, 42 links), refined by paired trials vs. no-skill and previous graph version.

PassNet: one benchmark-level graph for FX-graph inspection, pattern matching, semantics-preserving rewrites, Triton implementation, and performance diagnosis; refined over training instances with screening and sub-agent batches.
Fixed Codex harness with GPT-5.5 backbone at xhigh reasoning; only variable is presence of DisCo skills; skill construction budget separate from matched downstream running budget.

MLE-bench: all 75 competitions, Any-Medal via official grader, 3 runs, <=24 GPU-hours/task at run time. PaperBench: all 20 papers with official replication grader. FrontierCS: all 188 Agent Track tasks via Harbor, 5h/task, 2 CPUs/4GiB. PassNet: 200-sample eval list on A100-40GB with AS Score, G-Mean speedup, correctness, Fast_1.
Same Codex/GPT-5.5 agent without skills (primary control).
Public leaderboard systems: MLE-bench (Famou-Agent 2.0, AIBuildAI, CAIR MARS+, MLEvolve, R&D-Agent), FrontierCS (Claude Code with Opus 4.8 / Qwen3.7 Max, Gemini CLI).

key_findings.finding: Adding distilled skills to an unchanged agent yields large, consistent gains across four autonomous-research benchmarks under matched backbone, harness, and run-time budget.
key_findings.evidence: MLE-bench Any-Medal rises 31.11% -> 72.89% (+41.78 pts, +134.3% relative) over 75 competitions; PaperBench 29.45 -> 39.59 (+34.4% relative, better on 18/20 papers); FrontierCS 70.63 -> 77.14 (+9.2%, paired bootstrap 95% CI [3.41, 9.83]); PassNet AS Score 1.343 -> 1.5313 (+14.0%).

key_findings.finding: Skill augmentation of a vanilla harness surpasses specialized state-of-the-art agent systems, indicating the knowledge layer is complementary to harness engineering.
key_findings.evidence: Codex+AREX-Skill scores 72.89% on MLE-bench vs. 64.44% for the best public leaderboard entry (Famou-Agent 2.0 on Gemini-3-Pro), and on FrontierCS beats Claude Code/Opus 4.8 (74.5) while using 4.47M vs 14.72M tokens per task, Pareto-dominating on score, tokens, steps, and tool calls.

key_findings.finding: Gains concentrate where unguided exploration fails: hardest tasks and low-baseline tasks benefit most.
key_findings.evidence: MLE-bench High tier goes 13.33% -> 62.22% (+48.89 pts, 366.8% relative) vs +43.94 on Low; FrontierCS tasks scoring below 50 without skills rise from 19.43 to 45.99 mean (+26.56) with 30 crossing the 50 threshold; PaperBench ftrl rises 1.50 -> 17.17 (11.4x) and rice 7.94 -> 48.51 (6.1x) while already-strong tasks gain ~2 points.

key_findings.finding: The improvement comes from guidance content rather than from skills merely inducing more compute or search.
key_findings.evidence: On FrontierCS, per-task gains are essentially uncorrelated with extra usage (Spearman rho 0.006 tokens, 0.014 steps, 0.015 tool calls), and gains persist on the 102 tasks without sub-agent use (+5.54 mean paired gain).

key_findings.finding: Skills mainly reduce invalid or stalled outcomes, but poorly matched retrieval can occasionally hurt strong baseline tasks.
key_findings.evidence: On PassNet, failed samples drop 14 -> 5 (-64.3%) and correctness rises 81.35% -> 90.76%, exceeding TorchInductor's 1.419 AS Score; conversely two PaperBench tasks regress (sample-specific-masks 57.11 -> 52.04, stay-on-topic 32.31 -> 27.79), both above the no-skill average, and PassNet construction analysis found an overly absolute skill rule blocking a valid conv3d rewrite.
